theme: Church discipline; lawsuits; marriage and sexuality
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 5:1-7:40. This is a long reading on hard topics: sexual sin in the church, lawsuits, sexuality, and marriage. Read it carefully and with humility. Notice that Paul grounds his commands in the gospel: you were washed, you were bought with a price.
settingTheScene: Paul now deals with specific problems reported to him. Chapter 5 concerns a man living in sexual immorality of a kind that even pagans would not tolerate, and the church’s proud tolerance of it. Chapter 6 addresses believers suing each other in pagan courts, and sexual sin. Chapter 7 begins his response to the church’s letter, “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote,” with a long discussion of marriage, singleness, and divorce. Corinth had a reputation for sexual license, and some believers swung to the opposite extreme of asceticism.
observation: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (5:7).
“For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?” (5:12).
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (6:11).
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (6:19-20).
“Each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another” (7:7).
“Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him” (7:17).
“You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (7:23).
interpretation:
A man is living with his father’s wife, and the church is arrogant instead of grieving. Paul tells them to remove him from their fellowship, “to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.” Church discipline has a redemptive goal. He uses the picture of leaven: “a little leaven leavens the whole lump.” And the gospel is the basis: “Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.” The church is to be what it already is in Christ. Paul distinguishes judgment of those inside the church from those outside; God judges outsiders.

In chapter 6, Paul rebukes believers who take each other to court before unbelievers. “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” Surely they can settle ordinary matters. It is better to be wronged. Then he lists the unrighteous who will not inherit the kingdom of God: the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, men who practice homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers, swindlers. “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” The words “such were some of you” are among the most hopeful in the Bible. No one is beyond the reach of the gospel, and no one is allowed to stay as they were.

Paul rejects the slogan “All things are lawful for me.” Not all things are helpful. The body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. God raised the Lord and will raise us. Our bodies are members of Christ. “Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.” Then: “Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” This is the basis for Christian ethics: we belong to Christ, body and soul.

In chapter 7, Paul addresses marriage and singleness. Marriage is good, and sexual relations within marriage are a duty and a gift, to be mutual. He speaks of his own singleness as a gift: “Each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.” To the married he gives the Lord’s command that a wife should not separate from her husband, nor a husband divorce his wife. If a believer has an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay, they should stay. “But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved.” Christians differ on what this means for divorce and remarriage: some hold that 7:15 allows remarriage after desertion, and others hold stricter or looser positions. Pastoral care and prayer are essential.

The chapter has a repeated principle: “Let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him.” Whether married, single, circumcised, or slave, we serve the Lord where he has placed us. Paul urges single believers to consider the advantage of undivided devotion, but this is a counsel, not a command. And “the appointed time has grown very short.” The form of this world is passing away. Hold earthly relationships with an eye on eternity.
connection: Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 22:30 forbid the sin in chapter 5. Exodus 12 describes the Passover. Matthew 18:15-20 gives the process of discipline. 2 Corinthians 2:5-11 may describe the repentance of this man. Genesis 2:24 is quoted in 6:16. Ephesians 5:22-33 speaks of marriage as Christ and the church. Matthew 19:1-12 is Jesus’ teaching on divorce and singleness. Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage. Romans 6:1-14 and 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8 teach holiness. Daniel 7:22 says the saints will judge.
application:
Say 6:11 aloud and put your name in it. You were washed, sanctified, and justified.

Ask where you belong to yourself instead of Christ. Offer your body to him.

If you are single or married, ask God to show you how to serve him fully where you are. Pray for someone in a hard marriage.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being your Passover lamb.
Thank him that you were washed, sanctified, and justified.
Ask him to help you flee what harms you.
